final_answer:
Let
\[
\Delta_\tau(\lambda)=\lambda^2+a\lambda+1+(b+c\lambda)e^{-\lambda\tau},
\qquad a>0,\ b,c\ge 0.
\]

We determine when no root can lie in \(\{\operatorname{Re}\lambda\ge 0\}\) for any \(\tau\ge0\).

For \(\lambda=i\omega\), \(\omega>0\), write \(\theta=\omega\tau\). Then
\[
0=\Delta_\tau(i\omega)
=1-\omega^2+ia\omega+(b+ic\omega)(\cos\theta-i\sin\theta).
\]
Equating real and imaginary parts gives
\[
b\cos\theta+c\omega\sin\theta=\omega^2-1,
\]
\[
c\omega\cos\theta-b\sin\theta=-a\omega.
\]
The matrix of this system has squared norm \(b^2+c^2\omega^2\), so such a \(\theta\) exists exactly when
\[
(\omega^2-1)^2+a^2\omega^2=b^2+c^2\omega^2.
\]
Putting \(x=\omega^2>0\), this becomes
\[
q(x):=x^2+(a^2-c^2-2)x+1-b^2=0. \tag{1}
\]

Conversely, every positive solution \(x\) of (1) yields a suitable \(\theta\), hence a delay \(\tau=\theta/\sqrt{x}\), producing the imaginary root \(i\sqrt{x}\).

Also, \(\lambda=0\) is never a root since
\[
\Delta_\tau(0)=1+b>0.
\]

Thus imaginary-axis roots occur for some delay exactly when \(q\) has a positive root.

It remains to note that this condition completely characterizes delay-independent stability. At \(\tau=0\),
\[
\Delta_0(\lambda)=\lambda^2+(a+c)\lambda+(1+b),
\]
whose roots have negative real parts because \(a+c>0\) and \(1+b>0\).

Moreover, if \(\operatorname{Re}\lambda\ge0\) and \(\Delta_\tau(\lambda)=0\), then
\[
|\lambda^2+a\lambda+1|
=|b+c\lambda|e^{-\tau\operatorname{Re}\lambda}
\le b+c|\lambda|.
\]
Since the left side is at least \(|\lambda|^2-a|\lambda|-1\), all roots in the closed right half-plane lie in a fixed bounded region, uniformly in \(\tau\). Therefore the number of right-half-plane roots can change as \(\tau\) varies only through an imaginary-axis root. Hence the locus is disjoint from the closed right half-plane for every delay exactly when \(q\) has no positive root.

Now classify this condition. Set
\[
d=a^2-c^2-2.
\]
Then
\[
q(x)=x^2+dx+1-b^2.
\]

- If \(0\le b<1\), then \(1-b^2>0\). The quadratic has no positive root exactly when
  \[
  d>-2\sqrt{1-b^2},
  \]
  i.e.
  \[
  a^2>c^2+2-2\sqrt{1-b^2}.
  \]

- If \(b=1\), then
  \[
  q(x)=x(x+d).
  \]
  There is no positive root exactly when \(d\ge0\), i.e.
  \[
  a^2\ge c^2+2.
  \]
  The zero at \(x=0\) is harmless because \(\lambda=0\) is not a root.

- If \(b>1\), then \(q(0)=1-b^2<0\) while \(q(x)\to+\infty\), so \(q\) has a positive root.

Therefore,
\[
\boxed{
\mathcal R(a,b,c)\cap\{\operatorname{Re}\lambda\ge0\}=\varnothing
\iff
\begin{cases}
0\le b<1,\quad a^2>c^2+2-2\sqrt{1-b^2},\\[2mm]
\text{or}\\[1mm]
b=1,\quad a^2\ge c^2+2.
\end{cases}}
\]
